page: Microsoft Azure FX32ms_v2 is a high-frequency, memory-dense virtual machine built on Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. The instance features a 4.2 GHz Intel Xeon 8573C processor with 32 dedicated vCPUs derived from 16 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. It provides 260 MB of L3 cache and 672.0 GB of total RAM, yielding an unusually large ratio of 21.0 GB of memory per vCPU. The server does not bundle local ephemeral storage, requiring remote storage volumes for persistent data, and does not include discrete hardware accelerators.

Benchmark evaluations highlight strong computational and data transfer capabilities. The instance scored 2309.0 in single-core Geekbench testing, placing it in the top 10 percent of evaluated systems, alongside a Geekbench multi-core score of 18624.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 52508.62. Memory throughput is notable, reaching 241.38 GB/sec in uncached large-block read testing and 137.05 GB/sec in large-block writes. Data compression performance is also robust, with single-threaded gzip throughput reaching 34.79 GB/sec and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression achieving 225.42 GB/sec.

Hardware vector and matrix capabilities are expanded through Intel AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions) and AVX-512 feature sets. While these CPU-based instruction sets allow small-model LLM text generation to achieve 295.13 tokens/sec, large models like 70B show constrained generation rates of 2.74 tokens/sec due to the lack of dedicated GPUs. The primary tradeoff of the instance architecture is the total reliance on attached network storage for disk I/O, meaning disk performance is tied entirely to network bandwidth and storage tier selection.

In terms of qualitative resource allocation, the high RAM-to-core ratio enables organizations running per-core licensed enterprise software to maximize memory footprint while containing licensing footprints. The instance is suited for memory-intensive relational database engines, in-memory data processing frameworks, electronic design automation (EDA), and CPU-intensive engineering simulations.
